segments.narration: The Thames flooded this tunnel six times before it opened. Rotherhithe to Wapping, started 1825, four hundred metres of brick under a tidal river.
Nobody had tunnelled under a navigable river before. The bed was soft silt, dig in and the river poured through. Six men died in 1828.
Marc Brunel's answer was patented in 1818: an iron shield, divided into cells, one miner per cell, brickwork laid right behind as it crept forward.
Engineers long credited the idea to a dockyard pest: the shipworm, which bores through ship timber behind a hard shell, lining the hole as it goes.
It worked. Two million people a year paid a penny to walk under the Thames. Overground trains still run through Brunel's brick tube.

verdicts.claim: The Thames Tunnel, begun in February 1825 between Rotherhithe and Wapping and about 400 metres long, flooded six times during construction before opening on 25 March 1843.
verdicts.note: 83% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article, including 4 number(s)

verdicts.claim: A flood on 12 January 1828 killed six men, and Isambard Kingdom Brunel survived it.
verdicts.note: 78% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article, including 2 number(s)

verdicts.claim: Marc Brunel patented the tunnelling shield in January 1818; it was divided into compartments with one worker per cell and the brickwork was placed behind it as it advanced.
verdicts.note: 94% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article, including 1 number(s)

verdicts.claim: The shield's design is widely credited to the shipworm Teredo navalis, which bores through ship timber behind a hard shell and lines its burrow as it goes.
verdicts.note: The attribution itself is what the narration asserts, and it is well documented: the Brunel Museum records that Brunel saw Teredo navalis damage at Chatham Dockyard and says the inspiration is 'often suggested', and the Conchological Society traces the account to the naturalist J. G. Wood and draws the shell-lined-burrow parallel. The underlying inspiration is traditional, not established by any statement of Brunel's, and Wikipedia's Thames Tunnel article does not mention it at all, which is why the narration says only that engineers have long credited it.

verdicts.claim: The tunnel drew about two million pedestrians a year paying a penny, was converted to a railway in 1869, and has carried London Overground trains since 2010.
verdicts.note: 88% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article, including 2 number(s)
